analysis.one_liner: Restricts emergency orders that force fossil fuel plants to keep running and put the cost on power bills.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2026 by Senator Markey with four Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Energy Committee, where it has received no hearing, vote, or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill narrows a federal emergency power (Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act) that lets the government order fossil fuel power plants to keep running during grid emergencies, even over environmental rules. Under the bill, such orders could no longer block a plant's planned retirement unless a true emergency exists and the grid operator asks for the delay. It also requires a public hearing, a public docket, an analysis of alternatives and costs before an order is issued or renewed, and written notice to utility customers within 60 days about how the order affects their bills.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that pay electric bills, since emergency orders that force uneconomic fossil plants to run can add fuel, maintenance, and capital costs that flow into rates. Communities living near fossil plants also benefit from restored environmental protections and public input before orders are renewed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Electricity customers and communities near plants

how_it_helps.text: Bars emergency orders that prevent or delay a fossil plant's planned retirement, except when an emergency cannot be met any other way and the transmission organization requests the delay in writing.

Requires the commission to hold a public hearing, analyze whether the order will raise rates for customers, consider alternatives that minimize environmental harm, and consult state and local regulators before issuing or renewing an order.
Requires utilities to send customers written notice within 60 days of an emergency order, describing its impacts and expected costs such as added fuel, maintenance, capital, or labor costs.

Ends the current practice of issuing emergency orders 'with or without notice, hearing, or report' and treats orders for the same facility and a substantially similar emergency as renewals subject to full review.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel plant owners and operators, who would lose emergency orders that keep their plants running and earning revenue at customer expense. Grid operators would also lose a tool they can currently use without public process, though they retain a formal role in requesting retirement delays in genuine emergencies.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil plant owners and grid operators

drawbacks.text: In a severe grid emergency where no alternative supply exists, restricting the ability to quickly order plants online or delay retirements could raise the risk of outages; the bill's own narrow exception, which requires the grid operator to request the delay, acknowledges this reliability concern.

The new hearing, cost-analysis, and notice requirements add procedural steps to a tool designed for emergencies, which could slow response in fast-moving situations and add administrative work for utilities and the commission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is reliability versus cost and accountability. The bill keeps a narrow escape valve for true emergencies but removes the ability to use the emergency power routinely or repeatedly for the same plant, and it forces the costs of any emergency order to be published and disclosed to the customers paying them. For most ratepayers the benefits outweigh the procedural costs, though in rare extreme-weather events the slower process could matter.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote; Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced S. 4337 on April 16, 2026, joined by four Democratic cosponsors (Welch, Van Hollen, Merkley, and Blunt Rochester), with no Republican support.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day it was introduced, and no further action is recorded since then.

The bill amends Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act, the emergency authority the federal government has used to order fossil plants to run despite environmental limits, and would bar using that authority to block a plant's retirement except in a narrow emergency.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, fossil plant owners and operators, who keep their current access to emergency orders that keep their facilities running at customer expense; the bill has not advanced toward changing that status quo.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 4337 and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

for.name: Sens. Peter Welch, Chris Van Hollen, Jeff Merkley, and Lisa Blunt Rochester
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, its only recorded support.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats and no Republican cosponsors are recorded; the bill sits with the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no action since referral.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel power plant owners (coal, oil, and gas generators)
industries.note: The bill ends the ability to use federal emergency orders to keep their plants running, including to block planned retirements, cutting off a source of forced revenue. Those costs currently flow to electricity customers, so the industry's interest in the status quo runs against ratepayers.

They lose a no-notice emergency tool, but the bill gives them a formal role: a retirement can only be delayed in a true emergency if the transmission organization requests it in writing. Greater accountability and ratepayer notice also align with their public-service obligations.

By requiring consideration of alternatives that meet the emergency with minimal environmental harm, and by removing forced fossil operation, the bill favors cleaner resources competing to serve the grid in emergencies.

Utilities face new 60-day customer notice duties when an emergency order affects them, adding compliance work, but they are also the parties whose customers bear the order's costs and who benefit from transparent cost disclosure.

analysis.trajectory: With only five Democratic sponsors, a Republican-led committee, and no recorded action since referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or markup in this Congress and would probably die when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
